newsitem.title: Congo: Congo factions make rival claims to hold airport.
newsitem.headline: Congo factions make rival claims to hold airport.

text.p: Congo's president and his rival both claimed to hold Brazzaville airport on Thursday after heavy fighting for control of the prized target eased off.
President Pascal Lissouba's troops fought fiercely on Wednesday to hold the airport against an assault by "Cobra" militia of his enemy Denis Sassou Nguesso.
The fighting ended a week-old truce as well as hopes that a planned U.N. peacekeeping force would would arrive soon.
The United Nations made a firm truce and a demilitarised airport preconditions for its dispatch.
Fighting has paralysed the capital since early June, killing hundreds and splitting the city down the middle. The loss of the airport would be a serious blow to Lissouba's embattled forces.

"We have taken the airport," Ambroise Noumazalayi, Sassou's right-hand man, told French radio. He said that under the ceasefire accord, it should have been demilitarised but Lissouba had refused to budge.
"We decided not to leave this place to them because they used it to bring in arms and men," he said.
A spokesman for Lissouba said his men were still in control.
"Today the airport is well and truly in the hands of the regular army," he told Reuters by telephone.
"There was in incursion yesterday but it was repulsed and Sassou's bandits abandoned a tank with some dead in it."
Wednesday's long artillery battle sent many hundreds of civilians fleeing Brazzaville to safer suburbs on its northern and southern edges, the Red Cross said.
Panicky government troops assaulted French ambassador Raymond Cesaire, beat up his bodyguard and shot at escorts as they left Lissouba's palace after a meeting, witnesses said.
Cesaire, the only foreign envoy left, said on Thursday he intended to carry on working for now from his city-centre embassy, just 200 metres (yards) from the front line.
Sassou Nguesso, for 13 years Congo's one-party president until Lissouba defeated him in free elections in 1992, was to have run in next month's presidential elections.
The poll, in which he, Lissouba and city mayor Bernard Kolelas were main contenders, has been postponed.
Kolelas, whose own Ninja militia was involved in ethnic clashes in 1993 in which 2,000 people died, has stayed neutral this time and controls a southern section of town.
French troops evacuated thousands of foreigners through Brazzaville airport during the early fighting, but pulled out themselves last week.

France, its influence waning in neighbouring former Zaire and its troops under fire in the Central African Republic, said it would offer logistical support but no troops for a peacekeeping force for its former Congo colony.
Paris has announced a general review of its military links to former African colonies, where it has some 8,000 soldiers stationed. They have often intervened in local disputes.
